newsitem.title: GREECE: Greenpeace hails refinery protest as success.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace hails refinery protest as success.

text.p: Greenpeace on Thursday declared its blockade of Greece's largest oil refinery a success for creating a strong political and public reaction against oil pollution.
A Greek prosecutor charged 17 Greenpeace protesters over the blockade at the Motor Oil refinery near the Corinth Canal on Wendesday.
They were arrested after a raid by Coast Guard commandos ended a 24-hour blockade during which Greenpeace activists chained themselves to mooring buoys and loading cranes.
This is the first time that Greece has brought criminal charges against the international environmental group. The defendants include people from Britain, Austria and Germany.
If convicted on charges of trespass and hindering a public service company, they could face up to five years in jail.
Wednesday's military-type operation prompted heated reaction from several Greek political parties and the media, while local residents rallied to support the protesters.
"Our political target was achieved because we revealed the real face of Motor Oil and the oil industry. They don't care about the environment," Greenpeace activist Stelios Psomas said.
He said the Socialist government had ignored Greenpeace's demands for stricter oil pollution laws.
"We are more than pleased with the public support we got and I have a feeling we stirred up thousands who never dared to speak up against Motor Oil and Vardinoyannis," he said.
Motor Oil, which has an annual capacity of five million tonnes is jointly owned by Saudi Aramco and the Greek Vardinoyannis family.
The company, which employs about 1,300 people and had a 1994 turnover of around $750 million, defended its environmental record, saying it took more precautions than required by law.
But the decision to send in commandos wearing hoods and carrying machineguns prompted strong press reaction.
"This kind of reaction embarrasses our country internationally," a commentator said on popular Flash radio.
Three opposition parties condemned the operation and Merchant Marine Minister Stavros Soumakis offered an apology.
"I am honestly sorry if my orders to remove the activists peacefully were not followed and special forces were used," he told reporters.
The Left Coalition party brought the issue to parliament, where the Environment Ministry must formally respond next week to questions about its oil pollution record.

"We asked the government, instead of arrests and violence against environmental groups, to explain its refusal to push tough safety rules and adopt Greenpeace's proposals on oil pollution," the party said in a statement.
